listen: Good morning. This is The Daily Brief for Sunday, November 1. Our lead story comes from the courts. A federal judge on Saturday threw out Donald Trump's ten billion dollar lawsuit against The Wall Street Journal and media mogul Rupert Murdoch. The suit was over a story reporting on the president's ties to Jeffrey Epstein. The judge said the president was grasping at straws. The summary does not say whether an appeal is planned. Now the front page. In Atlanta, Secretary of State Marco Rubio is hosting the G20 foreign ministers' meeting. The focus is economic and security challenges, and Rubio has had a tough time getting officials on the same page. In sports, Jabari Smith Junior scored thirty points and Marcus Smart added twenty four as the Houston Rockets beat the Oklahoma City Thunder, one nineteen to ninety eight, on Saturday night. In tech, a trending GitHub project called claude-mem records what a coding agent does in a session, compresses it, and feeds the relevant context back into later sessions. It works with Claude Code and other agents. Now the sections. In tech and AI, Anthropic says it is committing a portion of its shares to a new Public Benefit Fund. Politics next. Virginia and Washington, D.C. have sued to block construction of a Trump arch, and a judge has asked both sides to agree on a briefing schedule. In world news, cost of living protests in several German cities turned violent, with shops looted, on the same day hundreds of thousands protested in France. In sports, Tom Nolan knocked out Renato Moicano in round three at UFC Vegas one twenty three, and Luana Santos won a unanimous decision at UFC Fight Night. Four Braves were also nominated for Gold Gloves. In Atlanta, Invest Atlanta is holding community meetings on a plan to extend six Tax Allocation Districts through twenty fifty five. In architecture, Snaptrude has launched an AI agent for BIM workflows, covering concept design through construction documentation. In science and nature, NASA has asked industry about commercial servicing for the Hubble Space Telescope. That is the brief. Have a good day. This is the Sunday edition. Here is the week in review. Anthropic files for IPO; elections in Brazil, Serbia, Israel. Anthropic filed an S-1 with the SEC for a proposed initial public offering (w27). In the same week it committed a portion of its shares to a new Anthropic Public Benefit Fund (w55) and expanded its GSA partnership to bring Claude to all levels of government (w56). The Lever read the filing and pointed to a blackmail warning among the risks (w52). For your tools: Opus 4.8 fast mode will be removed November 30, and users need to move to Opus 5.5 (w126). A beta Usage and Cost Analytics API also arrived (w103). Design skills for coding agents trended on GitHub (w5, w6, w127). In AEC, Snaptrude launched an AI agent for BIM workflows (w102). Abroad, Lula won a fourth term in Brazil over Flávio Bolsonaro (w1), who later arrived in Miami while facing investigations (w86). Vučić said his party lost Serbia's vote to a student-led movement (w2). Israel's election ended in deadlock (w132). A ceasefire across Ukraine's Kherson region let hundreds leave Oleshky (w125). The Ebola outbreak reached 10,000 patients (w54), and analytics firms linked North Korea to a $6.3 billion Binance hack (w122). At home, polls show Democrats ahead before the midterms (w60), and early voting in Georgia passed two million (w70). In Atlanta, MARTA began construction on its Cleveland-Metropolitan rapid transit project (w42), another Beltline segment broke ground (w68), and the Beltline revealed five options for connecting to MARTA rail (w138). The Rockets started 5-0 before losing to Dallas (w123), then beat the Thunder (w146). The 49ers traded for DeForest Buckner during their bye (w53), and the Braves exercised the options on Acuña and Albies (w101).

lead.title: 'Grasping at straws': Judge dismisses Trump suit against Wall Street Journal over Epstein letter
lead.note: A federal judge on Saturday threw out Donald Trump's $10 billion lawsuit against The Wall Street Journal and media mogul Rupert Murdoch. The case named both the newspaper and Murdoch as defendants. It targeted a story that reported on the president's ties to Jeffrey Epstein. In dismissing the case, the judge said the president was "grasping at straws." The ruling removes a high-profile legal dispute between a sitting president and a major newspaper from the court's docket. The summary does not say whether Trump will appeal, so that remains an open question for now. For readers, the main point is plain: the court rejected the claim, and the newspaper and its owner no longer face the suit, at least for now.
